before.heading: Make an availability call distinct from a rental reservation.
before.intro: A rental website still has a useful job when equipment is first-come, first-served. Your page can help customers choose what to ask about, understand what the call establishes and prepare for collection and return.
before.customerQuestion: If skis are available when I call, will a set be held for my visit?

decisions.label: State what the inquiry establishes
decisions.body: Put the actual no-reservations or holding policy beside equipment choices and the telephone route. A booking-style button should not suggest that an availability answer creates a reserved set.

decisions.label: Identify the rental being discussed
decisions.body: Separate daily and season arrangements, package contents and individual items. Someone needing only boots should be able to find that discussion without assuming a complete package or season agreement applies.

decisions.label: Explain the handoff and changes
decisions.body: Use current instructions for fitting preparation, collection and return. Distinguish pickup from the day of use, and explain whom to contact about a changed rental period without implying an automatic extension.

ownerInputs: Current package contents, separate items and seasonal terms.
Exact availability-check and reservation wording used by staff.
Approved fitting, pickup and return instructions with an update owner.
before.sourceBridge: Lake Placid Ski & Board publishes first-come rentals without reservations, telephone availability checks, and daily and season offerings. Its shop is at 2532 Main Street, Lake Placid; proximity to Whiteface does not imply mountain admission is included.
before.limits: Seasonal facts come from the owner and need an agreed publishing window. Website care does not monitor stock or decide current terms. Live inventory, reservations, agreements and fitting systems need separate scope; an informational page can support telephone inquiries.

before.lead: Ordering an item from a shop and asking it to personalize something you already own can require different first steps. I help Lexington and Fayette County businesses explain those routes before customers choose a design or request a quote.
before.decisionTitle: Identify the item before approving its personalization.
before.decision: For an illustrative engraving business, a design choice does not establish that a customer-supplied object is suitable for the work. The Lexington example below explicitly invites customers to bring an item, send a photograph or describe a project. I can clarify the difference between shop-supplied products and supplied-item inquiries around an existing contact route, or build a fuller service introduction. The owner determines what can be accepted; the website should preserve that review before presenting the requested personalization as agreed work.

scopes.check: A customer with their own cup can ask about that item without being treated as though they selected a product from your catalog. Spelling approval does not stand in for item acceptance.
